The Garganey (Spatula querquedula) shows marked sexual size dimorphism, with adult males attaining a maximum body mass of 342 grams [Wwi = 342 grams], while females are considerably lighter, reaching an ultimate wet weight of just 310 grams [Wwi = 310 grams]. This divergence is typical among dabbling ducks, where males often outweigh females by approximately ten percent, a pattern linked to sexual selection and the energetic demands of courtship displays. In terms of early development, the freshly laid eggs weigh only 27 grams [Ww0 = 27 grams], representing a substantial initial investment relative to the female's own body size. Neonates emerge from incubation at a markedly lower wet weight at birth of 21 grams [Wwb = 21 grams], indicating that roughly twenty-two percent of the initial egg mass is lost as metabolic water and shell material during embryonic development.

The timing of hatching is tightly coupled to thermal conditions during incubation. When eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which approximates the lower end of the natural incubation range for temperate Anseriformes, the age at birth is roughly 22 days [ab = roughly 22 days]. Field observations, however, indicate that the natural incubation period can vary substantially, with clutches hatching anywhere between 33 and 37 days depending on nest attendance patterns and ambient thermal fluctuations. This sensitivity to temperature highlights the vulnerability of ground-nesting waterfowl to climatic variability, as prolonged or intermittent cooling can delay development and reduce hatching success. The relatively short incubation duration compared to larger anatids reflects the Garganey's status as a small-bodied, rapidly developing species adapted to ephemeral wetland habitats.

Under the controlled thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which correspond to the active metabolic range typical of incubating and brooding adults, the post-hatching developmental schedule of the Garganey follows a compressed but predictable trajectory. Fledging, defined here as the achievement of sustained flight and nutritional independence from the parents, occurs approximately 37.75 days after hatching [tx = approximately 37.75 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid progression from a downy chick weighing only 21 grams [Wwb = 21 grams] to a fully flighted juvenile is energetically demanding and is facilitated by the high-protein invertebrate diet that parents provide during the brief nestling period. The timing of fledging is critical for this long-distance Palearctic migrant, as broods must be capable of sustained flight before the autumn migration to sub-Saharan Africa commences.

The onset of reproductive capability in the Garganey unfolds across two distinct milestones, both measured at the species' characteristic active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The age at puberty, reflecting the attainment of full gonadal maturation and the ability to produce viable gametes, is estimated at 113 days after hatching [tp = 113 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. However, the actual age at first successful reproduction in the wild is considerably later, occurring approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between physiological maturity and first brood production is a common life-history strategy among migratory waterfowl, allowing young birds to complete their first northward migration, establish a breeding territory, and accumulate sufficient body reserves before committing to the high energetic costs of egg formation and incubation.

The Garganey exhibits a moderate annual reproductive output typical of small-bodied dabbling ducks. Females typically lay between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 14 eggs per clutch], with most nests containing approximately 8 to 10 eggs. This species produces a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a pattern that reflects the short breeding window available in temperate and boreal wetlands during the northern summer. The maximum lifespan under natural conditions, recorded in wild populations and estimated at 19.8 years [am = 19.8 years], is remarkably long for a duck of this body size, rivaling larger congeners at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Basal metabolic rate measurements at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 402 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 402 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the high metabolic demands of a small-bodied, active forager that undertakes one of the longest migrations of any dabbling duck.
